title: Tenali Raman Tale 107 (தமிழ்)

full_text:
An arrogant foreign king, seeking an excuse to declare war upon Vijayanagara without appearing aggressive, sent an impossible diplomatic ultimatum to King Krishnadevaraya:
'To our brother Krishnadevaraya:
We demand that your famous engineers dig an abundant, fresh-water stone well atop the highest, sharpest rocky granite peak of Mount Matanga within thirty days, so that our passing caravans may drink!
If you fail, we shall consider your empire negligent of regional trade and declare war!'

The King’s master masons and hydrologists were in despair:
'Maharaj, Mount Matanga is a solid, towering pyramid of barren granite! There are no underground aquifers on a peak two thousand cubits above the valley! To dig a well there is an absolute impossibility!'

King Krishnadevaraya sat with a heavy heart, dreading an unjust war.
Tenali Raman stepped forward with a smile:
'Maharaj, reply to the foreign king that his royal request has been enthusiastically accepted, and that I, Tenali Raman, shall personally lay the foundation stone of the well on Mount Matanga!'

Two weeks later, Tenali Raman arrived as an imperial envoy at the foreign king's palace.
Tenali bowed with majestic courtly elegance and announced:
'Your Majesty! Emperor Krishnadevaraya has mobilized five hundred stone masons, twenty water diviners, and three hundred bullocks to construct your magnificent well atop Mount Matanga!
The summit has been surveyed, and the sacred coordinates are marked!'

The foreign king was stunned: 'Truly? You have begun digging into solid granite?'
Tenali replied with immense enthusiasm:
'Indeed! But as Your Majesty knows, our ancient architectural treatises state that a well dug upon a high mountain peak cannot stand unless its foundation is anchored with **Mountain-Base Granite Clay** supplied by the requesting monarch!
We have brought fifty pack-camels to your gates.
I pray thee, Your Majesty: order your servants to shovel three hundred cartloads of Mountain-Base Granite Clay from the sky into our sacks, so we may lay the foundation of your well tomorrow morning!'

The foreign king stared in bewilderment:
'Shovel granite clay from the sky? Art thou mad? How can anyone shovel stone from empty air?'

Tenali smiled with dazzling, razor-sharp wit:
'Precisely, Your Majesty!
If your kingdom cannot shovel granite clay from empty clouds, how can Vijayanagara dig an aquifer well atop a barren mountain peak?
When a king makes an impossible demand to manufacture an excuse for war, he must provide the impossible materials to build his folly!'

The foreign king realized he had been completely outmatched in intellect and diplomacy.
He laughed in admiration, withdrew his ultimatum, and signed a perpetual treaty of peace with Vijayanagara, while Tenali returned home having averted a war with a handful of wit.
moral: Demands to perform impossible geographic feats are countered by requiring the impossible foundation stones to begin. [TA]
